coherence.reasons: Both follow a clean line from diagnosis to sized levers to sequence, and both governing thoughts match their summaries and slide titles. X's hierarchy holds together throughout: labor is called the third-largest of four drivers, the 8% cut is rejected because of shrink, and the residual hours lever is limited to the most-staffed stores, where its own quartile data (Q4 only 0.1 pp below Q3) says hours buy little. Y has internal tensions. It calls labor the 'smallest cost line that rose' and the 'smallest cause' although its own waterfall shows occupancy smaller. It labels the 8% cut the wrong move for giving back half its saving to shrink, then relies on the same full 8% cut for $8.1M of its base case. And that base case assumes about $6.1M of extra shrink (roughly 0.43 pp), which would breach its own gate of chain shrink not above 2.6% after the cut.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend a defensible, sized plan: prune losing promotions, reprice delivery, exit the nine stores, grow private label, restore shrink controls, and cut hours later. Y weighs trade-offs more explicitly. It nets lost volume out of the promotion reset, treats only 65% of shrink as responsive to staffing, gives a break-even for the fee change (a 12% fall in online sales), builds a stress case, and sets five gates with thresholds and fallbacks, including a covenant fallback and a ValuMart comparable-sales guard. It also admits the base case reaches only 2.7%. X's judgment on labor is better: a roughly 4% cut confined to the best-staffed stores after a gate, rather than Y's full 8%. But X's headline rests on optimistic sizing, with no volume loss on promotions and every quartile reaching 2.3% shrink, and it has fewer contingencies. Y's weaknesses are leaning on the full 8% cut and on a second wave taking promotions to about 21%, below the FY2023 level, in the face of ValuMart, though both are gated. On balance Y weighs alternatives and trade-offs slightly better.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the bridge, the $10.4M e-commerce drag, the $2.5M fee gain and the $6.6M store-exit gain correctly, and both reject the e-commerce team's 6.1% claim. X has no numerical errors I could find. It engages the category team's claim quantitatively (the 1.6 pp comparable-sales gain pays for only 2.3 pp of promotional share) and uses the quartile data to argue where hours can safely come out. Its weak points are optimistic assumptions: the full 14 pp recovered on all 5 pp of promotional share with no volume loss, shrink at 2.3% in every quartile despite theft, and no shrink cost on its own 4.2% hours cut. All but the last are disclosed. Y's sizing is more conservative and its assumptions are labelled (25% lost volume, 65% of shrink responsive), and it adds the useful point that $9.8M of the $14.3M labor increase simply followed sales. But Y misstates labor as the smallest rising cost line when occupancy is smaller, dismisses the category claim without analysis, and its base case contradicts its own shrink gate. Net: X is slightly cleaner on errors and inferences; Y is more cautious on assumptions.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise the wage-inflation diagnosis with a quantified bridge. Both acknowledge the wage rate rise is real but was absorbed by productivity, and both show management's plan nets to roughly nothing by FY2028 after shrink and the 2027 wage rise. X's handling of the action follows the evidence more closely: it stops the 8% cut, restores rotation and receiving in lean stores, and keeps only a roughly 4% cut confined to the best-staffed stores after a shrink gate. Y keeps management's full 8% cut, only moved to last. It accepts about $6M of extra shrink and leaves customer response uncounted, a gap it had itself flagged against management's plan. Without that step its plan reaches only 2.1%. Y's gating and netting keep it within the conditionally defensible range, but it updates less than the shrink-by-quartile evidence warrants.

overall.reasons: The two documents are close: same diagnosis, same core levers, and both get near 3.0% only conditionally. Y gives the board better risk management, with conservative sizing, a stress case, explicit gates and fallbacks. X gives a more internally consistent answer to the central question of what to do about labor: its residual hours lever is smaller and targeted where the evidence says it is safe, and its diagnosis has no factual slips. Y's reliance on the full 8% hours cut is a material weakness for a board presentation, because that is the move its own analysis discredits and its base case would trip its own shrink gate. X's optimistic promotion and shrink sizing is the counterweight, which is why the margin is only slight.
